headline: Younger-generation investors tend to chase fads — crypto, AI, chip stocks — advisors encouraging discipline without fully restricting exposure
reasoning: Mann observes that younger beneficiaries typically want more aggressive, thematic positioning — often in trending areas like crypto, AI, and semiconductor stocks. The approach he recommends is not to prohibit this entirely but to give the younger generation a controlled environment (e.g. one entity or a ring-fenced allocation) to demonstrate their investment thinking, using it as an education journey. The broader portfolio, particularly for parents near or in retirement, needs to be managed conservatively to preserve capital and generate income.
quote: The next generation is always going to want to be a bit more aggressive and often follow fads, whether it's crypto, AI, chip stocks and so forth. We'd sort of encourage clients not to jeopardize their future with it, but depending on how much is there, you get them involved. Maybe if there's one entity that it's like, you know, you let them get started, it's okay. Show us how you would invest, then that can be the education journey of us working with them around. Why you perhaps need to be a bit more sensible for the parents, and then actually why the kids need that longer term plan.

headline: AI and shifting markets are prompting older wealth holders to involve younger generations in investment decisions earlier, including responsible investment preferences, even before transferring assets
reasoning: Mann observes that AI and market volatility are creating a new dynamic where older family members want next-generation input on how money is invested — including a tilt toward responsible investing — even if the actual transfer is deferred. This is seen as a positive development that sets expectations and avoids nasty surprises. The education journey is being formalised, with advisers working with both generations simultaneously.
quote: What we're finding is that now they've realized that with AI, with changes in markets, they want the next generation to have some say in how the money will be invested, even if they're not getting it now. So we're finding that they might be holding off on transferring it, but they're now letting the children have more of a say, whether it's in the types of investments or whether it's in responsible investment for the first time.
episode_title: Pass the wealth, not the problems | the advisory

headline: Geopolitical volatility — especially oil price shocks — is causing older wealth holders to pause intergenerational transfers, while budget tax changes are accelerating estate-planning conversations
reasoning: Angus Mann notes that early-March geopolitical events (Iran situation, oil price fears) triggered older family members who remembered the 1970s oil shocks to freeze transfer plans. However, the subsequent federal budget changes to trust taxation have re-energised estate-planning discussions. The combination of macro volatility and tax reform is making families more aware that wealth transfer timing is consequential and that long-term plans need to be stress-tested against market moves.
quote: Back in sort of early March, after the Iran situation started, a lot of the older family members who remembered the oil shocks of the 70s suddenly put a stop to everything. No, no, I'm going to eat everything for myself. Then once the budgets come, I think it's really highlighted the need for the conversation around how and when you transfer to the next generation.
episode_title: Pass the wealth, not the problems | the advisory

headline: Superannuation does not pass via a will — binding death benefit nominations, preferably non-lapsing, are essential to ensure super goes where intended
reasoning: Mann highlights a common misconception: superannuation is not governed by a will, so without a valid binding death benefit nomination the superannuation trustee has discretion over where the money goes, which may not align with the member's wishes. He recommends non-lapsing nominations where possible and stresses that nominations should be regularly reviewed. This is particularly important for large superannuation balances that form a significant part of intergenerational wealth transfer.
quote: Still something surprises a lot of people that you're super. Where your super goes isn't dictated by your will. So it's really important to make sure you have those binding death nominations in place, preferably non lapsing depending on how long it's going to be. But review it. But if you don't have those in place the super trustee can choose where the money goes and it may not be where you expect.
episode_title: Pass the wealth, not the problems | the advisory

headline: Budget changes to trust taxation are forcing families to rethink estate-planning strategies, with testamentary trusts gaining prominence as an alternative structure
reasoning: Mann explains that many families had pre-emptively placed assets into trusts expecting to do estate planning while still alive, but the budget changes have revealed drawbacks to that approach. As a result, families are reconsidering the timing and structure of wealth transfer. Testamentary trusts have become a major topic of conversation, and families are realising they have more flexibility about when and how to pass wealth to younger generations rather than feeling compelled to transfer everything at death.
quote: The main change has really been around the changes to how trusts are taxed. And so a lot of families that thought that they'd sort of do their estate planning ahead of time. Put it into a trust. Well, I, still alive, suddenly realize that there can be some drawbacks on that, and they're really having to rethink about when they pass it on.

headline: ESG and responsible investing adoption among philanthropic families tends to stall during periods of market stress, mirroring the COVID-era pullback
reasoning: Angus Mann observes that families with philanthropic portfolios who favour ESG and responsible investing tend to put those preferences on hold during volatile or uncertain market periods. This pattern was seen acutely during COVID, when interest in sustainable investing collapsed almost overnight before rebounding, and the same dynamic is playing out again now. He frames this as a recurring behavioural pattern rather than a structural shift away from ESG.
quote: The biggest change we actually see is that a lot of families who often want ESG, a responsible investment in their portfolios, they really sort of put that on hold through these periods when Covid, up until Covid, there was a big uptake in interest in sustainable investing. Covid came, everyone almost abandoned that overnight. And then it's come back since the same thing happens through periods like this as well.

headline: Angus Mann urges philanthropic investors to stay committed to their investment strategy through volatility rather than retreating to cash, citing the missed upside after Trump tariff-driven selloff
reasoning: Mann describes a common behavioural pattern where charitable investors become overly conservative during volatile periods, moving into cash and delaying investment decisions even when they have significant balances. He notes that advisors who held firm or added to equities after the Trump tariff-driven market pullback were rewarded. Retreating to cash typically means investors miss the subsequent recovery. His core message is that having and adhering to a long-term, diversified investment strategy is essential for foundations to meet their goals and distribution obligations.
quote: I think last year a lot of advisors did the right thing. That was the time we took advantage of cheaper prices and put more in. But we see this with every cycle and it can be a natural reaction. Things have gone down. People worry it's more dangerous. They want to pull it out. It's typically the time that you really need to stay committed and sort of, you know, be brave through that, knowing that markets do go in cycles. And unless we think that something structurally has changed, like it did for a bit during the GFC, you need to sort of stick to the plan through this.
episode_title: Why philanthropy needs an investment strategy too | the advisory

headline: Fixed income appeal has faded as higher cash rates compete with bond yields, and longer-duration bonds face headwinds in a higher-for-longer rate environment
reasoning: Angus Mann notes that fixed income has lost appeal for philanthropic and charitable investors as cash deposits offer competitive yields relative to bonds. In a higher-for-longer interest rate environment, longer-duration bonds are particularly vulnerable to capital losses. He also references the 2022-2023 period when bonds failed to provide their traditional diversification benefit, calling into question standard portfolio construction assumptions for foundations.
quote: So fixed incomes really sort of come off a lot, particularly when we're seeing if you can often get a better return, a better yield from money sitting in the bank. But if we're expecting interest rates to go higher, then, you know, bonds, your longer duration bonds, they're going to get hurt. And we've also seen particularly over 2022 2023. The bonds don't necessarily give you that.

headline: Australian government raises minimum annual distribution for private giving funds to 6%, prompting review of philanthropic investment strategies
reasoning: The Australian government has renamed private ancillary funds to 'giving funds' and raised the minimum annual distribution requirement from around 4-5% to 6% (down from the originally proposed 8%). This change will likely push some foundations to dial up investment risk to meet higher distribution requirements. Angus Mann emphasises that foundations should still maintain an appropriate, properly structured investment strategy rather than chasing returns. He notes that a sound investment strategy is the critical roadmap for any investor, including foundations, particularly during periods of market volatility.
quote: So in terms of the change, I think that some people will sort of look at it and go. We used to be able to give away 4 or 5. We'll have to give away 4 or 5% a year. Now at six, they'll probably try and dial up, sort of, you know, the risk a little bit, which can be of concern. You know, ultimately when a money, you put money into a foundation, it's not really yours anymore. You can't take it back. You've gotten your tax deduction. It's really the community needs money. And the main thing I think we want to make sure people are doing, we're reinforcing with clients, is that you still need to sort of, you know, remain appropriately invested if that's conservative, but really it's reminding everyone the need to have a proper investment strategy.

headline: Angus Mann urges investors to maintain broad equity exposure and avoid concentrating in thematic sectors, citing sharp drawdowns in South Korean stocks and semiconductors.
reasoning: Despite uncertainty, Mann argues the numbers support maintaining broad equity exposure.
